opus-5.5.text:
I think the most realistic path is not to pretend context will become infinite. Even if context windows keep growing, and they will, the work people want AI to do grows faster. A real research project or software project can run for weeks or months. You will never fit all of that into one window, and even if you could, attention over a huge undifferentiated context isn't the same as understanding it.

So the question becomes how the model manages its own state, the way humans do. When I work on a long project, I don't remember every keystroke. I keep notes, I write down what I've tried and why it failed, I organize files, I leave myself a to-do list. Most of my "memory" for the project lives outside my head, in artifacts I can go back to. I think models need to learn that same skill.

Concretely, I see a few pieces.

First, **external memory as a first-class tool.** The model should be able to write to and read from a file system, a notes file, a codebase, a database, and treat that as its working memory. This sounds simple, but the hard part is the judgment: what's worth writing down, at what level of abstraction, and when to go back and look something up instead of guessing.

Second, **summarization and compression of its own trajectory.** When the context fills up, the model should be able to distill what happened into a compact state, something like "here's the goal, here's what's done, here's what I learned, here's what's next," and then continue from that in a fresh context. Whether this works depends a lot on whether the model knows what will matter later, which is hard. Bad summaries lose the one detail that turns out to be critical.

Third, **decomposition and delegation.** A lot of long tasks can be broken into subtasks, each with a bounded context. One agent plans and coordinates, and others go off and do focused pieces and report back concise results. That's basically how human organizations deal with finite individual attention.

And the thing underneath all of it is **training for it.** You can scaffold these behaviors with prompts, and that gets you some distance. But I think the real progress comes when models are trained with reinforcement learning on long-horizon tasks where they actually have to manage their context to succeed, where the reward depends on finishing something that's impossible to do in one window. Then the model learns, from experience, what a good note looks like, when to compress, and when to start fresh.

So my short answer: finite context plus learned memory management. Not one giant brain that holds everything, but an agent that's good at keeping a clean desk, so to speak.

r001.rationale: It questions relying on ever-growing context windows, but does not discuss continually lengthening individual training segments.

r002.rationale: It proposes compressing the project history into a compact state and deciding what is worth retaining, which conveys discarding information that is not relevant later.

r003.rationale: It proposes using external memory and deciding when to look up information instead of guessing, conveying retrieval of relevant stored information.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the realistic path is not to pretend the context problem goes away. You can keep pushing context windows longer, and that helps, but it doesn't fundamentally solve the issue, because real work, the kind that takes a human weeks or months, generates far more information than any window can hold, and most of it you don't actually need at any given moment.

So the approach I find most realistic is to treat context as something the model actively manages, rather than something passively given to it. The model needs to learn what to keep, what to write down somewhere outside itself, and what to retrieve later. That's basically how humans work. I don't remember everything about a project I've been on for a year; I remember a compressed version, I keep notes, I have files, and I know where to look when I need the details.

Concretely, that means a few things. One is the model should be able to summarize its own trajectory, compress what it's done into something shorter, and keep working off that summary. Two is external memory, files, a scratchpad, tool outputs it can re-read, so the burden isn't all on the weights or the window. And three, maybe the most important, is that these should be learned behaviors, not just engineering hacks bolted on from the outside. If you train the model in environments where tasks genuinely require long horizons, it has to figure out how to manage its own state, because otherwise it fails. That's where I think reinforcement learning becomes essential, because you can't really supervise this with static data. You need the model to experience running out of room and learn what to do about it.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that there's a clean architectural trick that makes this disappear. I think it's more like, the model gets better at being an agent over its own context, and that skill compounds with everything else.

r001.rationale: The candidate says longer context windows help but do not solve the problem. It does not address continually lengthening individual training segments.

r002.rationale: It proposes managing context by choosing what to keep, compressing prior work, and relying on a shorter summary, which communicates omitting information not currently needed.

r003.rationale: It explicitly proposes retrieving information later from external memory, files, and tool outputs when the details are needed.

astra-6.text:
I think a realistic approach is to let the model manage an external memory. You don’t need to keep the entire history in the context window. You need to preserve the information that matters for the next step.

For example, if the model is working on a project, it can periodically write down what the goal is, what it has tried, what it has learned, and what remains unresolved. Then it can start with a fresh context, read those notes, and continue. More detailed information can stay in files and be retrieved when needed.

The hard part is deciding what to keep. A summary can lose a constraint or erase the reason an earlier approach failed, and then the model repeats the same mistake. So I would treat memory management as part of the task itself—something the model needs to learn and something we need to evaluate over long runs. A larger context window helps, but reliable progress also requires a good way to carry state across context windows.

r001.rationale: The response discusses external memory and context windows, but does not question extending individual training segments.

r002.rationale: It says the model need not keep the entire history and should preserve information that matters for the next step, which conveys selectively dropping irrelevant information.

r003.rationale: It proposes keeping detailed information in files and retrieving it when needed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a realistic approach is to separate how long a model works from how much context it keeps at any one time. You don’t necessarily need to put the entire history into an ever larger context window. You can let the model work for a while, write down the important state, and then continue with a fresh context.

The hard part is deciding what to preserve. A useful memory should capture the goal, what has been completed, what failed, and what still needs to be done. And the model should be able to retrieve the underlying details when necessary, rather than relying entirely on a summary that might have lost something important.

So I would think of it as an agent operating over persistent files and notes, with context serving as its working memory. That gives you a practical path toward longer work with finite context. But you also need ways to check progress, because otherwise the agent can keep running while gradually drifting away from the original task.

r001.rationale: The response rejects relying on an ever larger context window, but does not discuss or question continually lengthening individual training segments.

r002.rationale: It recommends carrying forward important state into a fresh context instead of the entire history, which communicates selectively dropping irrelevant information.

r003.rationale: It explicitly recommends retrieving underlying details when necessary rather than relying only on a summary.
